propositions.text: The Appellant appeals the RPD decision denying refugee protection, submits no new evidence, and requests no oral hearing.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying her claim for refugee protection. She has not submitted new evidence in support of her appeal and does not request an oral hearing.

propositions.text: The Appellant asks the RAD to reverse the RPD decision and send her file back for a hearing de novo.
propositions.quote: The Appellant asks the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to reverse the decision of the RPD and send her file back to the RPD for a hearing de novo.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant appeals the RPD decision denying refugee protection, submits no new evidence, requests no oral hearing, and asks the RAD to reverse and remit for a new hearing.

propositions.text: The RAD confirms the RPD decision that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection and dismisses the appeal.
propositions.quote: Pursuant to subsection 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. This appeal is dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD confirms the RPD decision denying refugee protection and dismisses the appeal.

propositions.text: The Appellant alleged before the RPD that she fears al-Shabaab and sympathizers because they believe her husband spied for the federal government.
propositions.quote: The Appellant alleged before the RPD that she fears al-Shabaab and its sympathizers in Somalia because they believe her husband spied for the federal government.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant alleged to the RPD a fear of al-Shabaab due to her husband's alleged spying.

propositions.text: The RPD rejected the claim for lack of credibility on key fear information and found residual evidence did not support refugee protection.
propositions.quote: By a decision dated February 16, 2016, the RPD rejected the claim finding that the Appellant lacked credibility with respect to the key information in her claim regarding a fear of persecution or harm from al-Shabaab. The RPD also found that the residual evidence did not support a claim for refugee protection.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD rejected the claim due to lack of credibility and insufficient residual evidence.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits that interpretation services were inadequate, affecting her natural right to be heard.
propositions.quote: On appeal to the RAD, the Appellant submits that the interpretation services provided to her throughout the process was inadequate and therefore affected her natural rights to be heard.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits the RPD was overzealous in scrutinizing interpreter-assisted testimony, ignoring likely interpretation errors.
propositions.quote: She further submits that the RPD was overzealous in scrutinizing her interpreter-assisted testimony in a scenario where it should have known that inconsistencies were likely the result of faulty interpretation services.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits the RPD misapprehended evidence regarding her clan.
propositions.quote: She also submits that the RPD misapprehended the evidence regarding her clan.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues inadequate interpretation affected her hearing, the RPD over-scrutinized interpreter-assisted testimony, and misapprehended clan evidence.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits procedural fairness issues like interpreter adequacy are reviewable on correctness standard.
propositions.quote: The Appellant notes that one of the grounds of her appeal can be broadly categorized under the breaching of principles of natural justice and procedural fairness, namely, whether or not the interpreter and his services were adequate. She submits that issues of procedural fairness are typically reviewable on the correctness standard.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits findings of fact and credibility are generally reviewed on reasonableness standard.
propositions.quote: With respect to the second ground of her appeal, relating to findings of fact and credibility, the Appellant submits that the appropriate standard of review is generally reasonableness.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant submits procedural fairness issues are reviewed on correctness, and fact and credibility findings on reasonableness.

propositions.text: The Federal Court of Appeal in Huruglica held the RAD applies correctness standard to intervene when RPD is wrong in law or fact.
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that the Federal Court of Appeal, in Huruglica, indicated that the role of the RAD is to intervene when the RPD is wrong in law, in fact or in fact and law; and this translates into an application of the correctness standard of review.

propositions.text: For findings of fact without credibility issues, RAD reviews RPD decisions on correctness standard.
propositions.quote: The Court held that, with respect to findings of fact (and mixed fact and law), which raises no issue of credibility of oral evidence, the RAD is to review RPD decisions applying the correctness standard.

propositions.text: RAD must analyze record and provide final determination, confirming or substituting RPD decision, or refer back if oral evidence hearing needed.
propositions.quote: It went on to indicate that after carefully considering the RPD decision, the RAD is to carry out its own analysis of the record to determine whether the RPD erred. The Court also stated that having done the above, the RAD is to provide a final determination, either by confirming the RPD decision or setting it aside and substituting its own determination of the merits of the refugee claim. It is only when the RAD is of the opinion that it cannot provide such a final determination without hearing the oral evidence presented to the RPD that the matter can be referred back to the RPD for redetermination.

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court of Appeal in Huruglica held RAD applies correctness standard to RPD errors, analyzes record, and provides final determination or refers back if needed.

propositions.text: RAD will analyze record to determine if RPD erred, applying correctness standard for fact findings without credibility issues.
propositions.quote: Considering the recent jurisprudence, the RAD will conduct its own analysis of the record to determine whether, as submitted by the Appellant, the RPD erred. Where no issue of credibility of oral evidence was raised, the RAD will apply a standard of correctness when assessing RPD findings of fact or of mixed fact and law.

propositions.text: Where credibility of oral evidence is raised, RAD defers to RPD findings based on RPD's advantage in assessing witnesses, case-by-case.
propositions.quote: Where the credibility of oral evidence was raised, the RAD will defer to certain findings of the RPD where the RPD enjoyed an advantage over the RAD in assessing the oral evidence of witnesses who appeared before it. The extent of this deference will be assessed on a case-by-case basis dependent upon the particular circumstances of the matter and in conjunction with the RAD's own analysis of the record as a whole.

propositions.text: Correctness standard applies to errors of law including breaches of natural justice or procedural fairness on appeal to RAD.
propositions.quote: In addition, the standard of correctness will be used for any error of law including a breach of natural justice or procedural fairness found in the RPD decision on appeal to the RAD.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD analyzes the record, applying correctness standard for fact findings without credibility issues, defers to RPD on credibility, and uses correctness for legal errors.

propositions.text: The Appellant relied on XXXX XXXX, a Somali community counselor, for interpretation and paperwork before having a lawyer.
propositions.quote: On appeal to the RAD, the Appellant points out that she fully relied upon XXXX XXXX, a counselor assigned to her by the Somali community, to interpret and translate for her when she first arrived in Canada because she did not speak English or French. She also points out that Mr. XXXX assisted her in completing all of her paperwork prior to having a lawyer, and she relied on Mr. XXXX to communicate with her lawyer after she retained one.

propositions.text: The Appellant later relied on her niece, who reviewed paperwork and found inconsistencies and concerns about Mr. XXXX's services.
propositions.quote: She notes that eventually she no longer relied on Mr. XXXX and instead relied on her niece, after they were reunited. The Appellant maintains that her niece reviewed her paperwork, noticed various inconsistencies, and expressed concern regarding Mr. XXXX prior services.

propositions.text: The Appellant was unable to correct her refugee application before hearing and sent a new narrative more true and complete than the BoC form.
propositions.quote: She maintains that she was unable to make corrections to her refugee application because she was unable to meet with her lawyer until just before her hearing; and simply sent in a new narrative that was more true and complete than the Basis of Claim Form (BoC) completed with the assistance of Mr. XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant relied on a counselor for interpretation and paperwork, later on her niece who found inconsistencies, and sent a new narrative before hearing.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits the interpreter at her hearing was Mr. XXXX, creating reasonable apprehension of bias affecting hearing integrity.
propositions.quote: The Appellant points out that Mr. XXXX was the interpreter at her hearing before the RPD. She submits that, given Mr. XXXX services to her and the concerns regarding his services to her, there is a reasonable apprehension of bias that would affect the integrity of the entirety of her hearing.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues the interpreter had personal interest to maintain reputation and might manipulate translation to cover past mistakes.
propositions.quote: She submits that the two primary indicators of potential bias in her case are the personal interest the interpreter has in any evaluation of the quality of his past services to her, and a prior professional relationship with her that may have ended on less than favourable terms. The Appellant argues that the interpreter had a personal interest in the outcome of the hearing, to her detriment, as his interest would be in maintaining his reputation by insisting or insinuating that his services are of the highest quality and that any problems with documentation had nothing to do with him and that the blame instead rested with her. She submits that a reasonable person could reasonably believe that the interpreter may manipulate his translation at the hearing to cover up the past mistakes he made during his prior professional relationship with her.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant alleges the hearing interpreter was Mr. XXXX, who had personal interest and bias, possibly manipulating translation to cover past mistakes.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits her claim was tainted by inability to correct misinterpretation and lack of assistance until too late.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that everything about her claim was tainted because she did not have the ability to correct any misinterpretation and she did not have any other assistance for that purpose until it was too late.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits her former counsel was negligent for not objecting to interpreter services and not informing her of rights.
propositions.quote: She submits that her former counsel should have objected to the services of the interpreter and informed her of her rights to competent interpretation.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues former counsel should have asked for a different interpreter, informed IRB, and requested adjournment when interpreter was same as before.
propositions.quote: She submits that her former counsel was negligent and therefore did not notice obvious inconsistencies such as different birthdays on different pages of her documents. She argues that careful counsel would have asked her about the inconsistencies and probably would have drawn attention to and inquired about the competency of the initial interpreter; her former counsel should have then asked for a different interpreter and informed the IRB of any changes through sworn declaration; and, when her former counsel noticed that the interpreter at the hearing was the same as the one who provided careless services at the documentation state, he should have objected and requested an adjournment to allow for the arrangement of a new interpreter.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits natural justice demands a new hearing with a different interpreter and Board member due to reasonable apprehension of bias.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that, given that the interpreter's role is pivotal in her hearing and there is a reasonable apprehension of bias on the part of the interpreter, natural justice would demand, at a minimum, that a new hearing be held with a different interpreter and Board member.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant alleges her claim was tainted by inability to correct misinterpretation, former counsel's negligence, and requests a new hearing with a different interpreter.

propositions.text: The Appellant was mistaken; the interpreter at hearing was not the same person who assisted with forms.
propositions.quote: The Appellant was wrong to believe that the person who assisted her in preparing her claim forms was also the interpreter at her hearing.

propositions.text: Documents show XXXX XXXX assisted with forms; XXXX XXXX XXXX was interpreter at hearing and testified as witness, not interpreter.
propositions.quote: It is clear from documents3 in the record that XXXX XXXX assisted the Appellant in the completion and interpretation of her forms. It is clear from the recording of the Appellant's hearing that XXXX XXXX XXXX was the interpreter at her hearing. Although XXXX XXXX was called as a witness at the Appellant's hearing by her counsel, he provided no interpretation or translation services at the hearing.

propositions.text: The Appellant's allegations about the hearing interpreter are without basis.
propositions.quote: Therefore, the Appellant's allegations regarding the interpreter at the hearing are completely without basis.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Appellant was mistaken; the hearing interpreter was different and her allegations about him are baseless.

propositions.text: At hearing, the Appellant confirmed her documents were complete, true, and understood, with questions and narrative interpreted in Somali.
propositions.quote: The Appellant, at her hearing, confirmed that the information she had provided in her documents was complete, true, and correct, and that she had understood the questions and the answers. The Appellant even indicated at her hearing that the questions were interpreted to her in the Somali language and her responses were recorded on the forms and read back to her in the Somali language. She indicated that her narrative was read back to her in the Somali language.

propositions.text: The Appellant had opportunity at hearing outset to correct or indicate inaccuracies but failed to do so.
propositions.quote: The Appellant had the opportunity at the outset of her hearing to make changes to the information in her forms before she confirmed that the information was accurate. She also had the opportunity at the outset of her hearing to indicate that the information in her forms was not accurate. She failed to make changes to the information in her forms and failed to indicate any inaccuracies at the outset of her hearing.

propositions.text: The Appellant's claim she was unable to make corrections before hearing is without merit.
propositions.quote: If the Appellant noticed errors in her forms before her hearing as she alleges, it would be reasonable to expect her to notify the RPD at the outset of her hearing. The RAD finds that the Appellant's assertion that she was unable to make corrections to the information in her forms is without merit.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Appellant confirmed her documents were accurate and had opportunity to correct errors at hearing but did not, so her claim of inability to correct is without merit.

propositions.text: The Appellant alleges former counsel was negligent for not noticing inconsistencies and not objecting to interpreter or requesting adjournment.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has alleged that her former counsel was negligent. She maintains that her former counsel did not notice obvious inconsistencies in her documents that careful counsel would have addressed before her hearing. She maintains that, when her former counsel noticed that the interpreter at the hearing was the same as the one who provided careless services at the documentation state, he should have objected and requested an adjournment to allow for the arrangement of a new interpreter.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant alleges former counsel was negligent for not addressing inconsistencies and not objecting to interpreter or requesting adjournment.

propositions.text: Counsel incompetence or negligence breaches procedural fairness only if specific, evidenced, and result likely different.
propositions.quote: Incompetence or negligence of counsel will amount to a breach of procedural fairness in only limited circumstances where: (a) the incompetence is sufficiently specific and clearly supported by evidence; and (b) there is a fairly arguable case that the result would have been different.

propositions.text: Courts require complaint to governing body as corroboration but not as requirement for incompetence allegation.
propositions.quote: Where counsel incompetence or negligence is alleged, the courts have required a complaint to the governing body as a form of corroborating evidence of the allegations. While complaints to a regulatory body may serve to corroborate claims of incompetence, they should not be perceived as requirements to making such an allegation.

propositions.text: Former counsel must be given notice and opportunity to respond to allegations against him.
propositions.quote: It is required that former counsel be given notice and an opportunity to respond to the allegations made against him.

paragraphs.summary: Counsel negligence breaches procedural fairness only if specific, evidenced, likely affecting result; complaint corroborates but is not required; counsel must be notified and respond.

propositions.text: No evidence shows Appellant complained to former counsel's regulatory body or gave him notice to respond to allegations.
propositions.quote: In this case, no evidence was presented to indicate that a complaint has been made by the Appellant against her former counsel to his regulatory body. More importantly, there is no indication that the Appellant's former counsel was advised of the complaint and allegations made against him.

propositions.text: The Appellant failed to meet requirement of giving former counsel notice and opportunity to respond to allegations.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that the Appellant has not met the requirement of giving her former counsel notice and an opportunity to respond to the allegations made against him.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no evidence of complaint or notice to former counsel and that the Appellant failed to give him opportunity to respond.

propositions.text: Correctness standard applies to errors of law including breaches of natural justice or procedural fairness on appeal to RAD.
propositions.quote: As noted above, the standard of correctness will be used for any error of law including a breach of natural justice or procedural fairness found in the RPD decision on appeal to the RAD.

propositions.text: Supreme Court of Canada states counsel conduct presumed reasonable; appellant must prove otherwise; hindsight not allowed.
propositions.quote: With respect to former counsel's conduct, the Supreme Court of Canada has stated, The analysis proceeds upon a strong presumption that counsel's conduct fell within the wide range of reasonable professional assistance. The onus is on the appellant to establish the acts or omissions of counsel that are alleged not to have been the result of reasonable professional judgment. The wisdom of hindsight has no place in this assessment.

paragraphs.summary: The correctness standard applies to legal errors; Supreme Court presumes counsel conduct reasonable and burden is on appellant to prove otherwise without hindsight.

propositions.text: The interpreter at hearing was not the same as who assisted with documents; allegation against counsel is baseless.
propositions.quote: As noted above, the interpreter at the hearing was not the same person who assisted the Appellant prepare her documents; therefore the Appellant's allegation that her former counsel failed to notice that that the interpreter at the hearing was the same as the one who provided careless services at the documentation state is without basis.

propositions.text: Former counsel addressed anomalies with Appellant at hearing and in submissions; this does not show negligence.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the Appellant's former counsel addressed anomalies in the Appellant's evidence with the Appellant at her hearing. He also addressed these anomalies in his submissions. In the RAD's view, former counsel's treatment of anomalies in the Appellant's evidence does not demonstrate negligence.

propositions.text: The Appellant failed to establish former counsel's conduct fell outside reasonable professional assistance.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that the Appellant has failed to establish that her former counsel's conduct fell outside the wide range of reasonable professional assistance.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the interpreter allegation against counsel baseless; counsel addressed anomalies and was not negligent; appellant failed to prove otherwise.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits the RPD misapprehended evidence about the XXXX clan's status and weakness.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that the RPD misapprehended the evidence that was given to it concerning the status of the XXXX clan when it found that there was no evidence of the XXXX being a weak clan.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues evidence shows XXXX and Hawiye are separate descent groups per UK report.
propositions.quote: She argues that evidence presented at the hearing should have alerted the RPD to the possibility that the XXXX and the Hawiye could accurately be described as "separate descent groups" within the meaning provided in a United Kingdom Country Information and Guidance report.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits third witness's assertion and second witness's description of clan affiliation are reasonable given dual definitions and alliances.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that the third witness's assertion that the Hawiye clan and the XXXX were separate clans fits within the current understanding of separate descent groups; that the second witness would have described the XXXX as "part of the Hawiye clan" was reasonable given the dual definitions of "group" in common usage and the reality that the Hawiye clan would have been the dominant clan in an alliance between itself and the XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant submits the RPD misapprehended evidence about the XXXX clan's status and reasonable clan affiliations per witnesses and UK report.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits RPD's misapprehension led to unreasonable conclusion of discrepancy between witnesses and documentary evidence.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that the RPD's misapprehension of the evidence concerning the status of the groups and the function of the clan alliances led it to unreasonably conclude that there was a discrepancy between the testimonies of the three witnesses, particularly the second witness and the documentary evidence, when there wasn't one.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits RPD wrongly precluded possibility that XXXX clan was small and minor despite alliance with Hawiye.
propositions.quote: She submits that this misunderstanding concerning the affiliation of the XXXX with the Hawiye clan led the RPD to preclude the possibility that the XXXX clan, due to its status in the hierarchy, may have had an alliance with Hawiye but was nonetheless still a small and minor clan.

propositions.text: The Appellant notes documentary evidence that XXXX clan is scattered and undercounted, supporting its minor status.
propositions.quote: She notes documentary evidence on the XXXX clan suggesting that the clan has been scattered and its numbers have not been properly accounted for.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits RPD's note that most documents do not list XXXX or XXXX clans supports their minor influence and population.
propositions.quote: She submits that the fact that the RPD noted that most documents that listed Somali clans and groups did not list either XXXX or XXXX, was evidence that reasonably indicated that her clan was not a major clan in terms of influence or population.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits RPD's misapprehension led to unreasonable finding that weakness of XXXX clan was not established and negative credibility inferences.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that the RPD's misapprehension of the evidence concerning the XXXX clan led it to unreasonably find that the weakness of the XXXX clan was not established while also making negative inferences with regards to her credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant submits RPD misapprehended clan evidence, leading to unreasonable findings on discrepancies, clan status, and negative credibility inferences.

propositions.text: The XXXX are part of or aligned with a majority clan, so the RPD was correct to find the Appellant not part of a weak minority clan.
propositions.quote: The evidence, in the RAD's view, demonstrates that the XXXX are a part of, or have aligned themselves, with a majority clan. Therefore, the RPD was not wrong to find that the Appellant had not established that she is part of a weak minority clan as alleged.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence shows the XXXX are a sub clan of Gorgate, a sub clan of the majority Hawiye clan.
propositions.quote: Documentary evidence indicates that the XXXX are a sub clan of the Gorgate, who are a sub clan of the majority Hawiye clan.

propositions.text: In Somalia, minorities can seek protection by attachment to stronger lineages; adoption of weak clans occurs.
propositions.quote: In Somalia, minorities can seek protection by attachment to stronger lineages, and the adoption of weak clans does occur.

propositions.text: Witness XXXX testified that the XXXX are not a big clan and are third in a branch after Hawiye and Gorgate.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX XXXX, a witness for the Appellant at her hearing and a member of the XXXX sub clan herself, testified that the XXXX are not a big clan. She indicated that every sub clan belongs to a clan and the XXXX are the third in a branch, after the Hawiye clan and the Gorgate sub clan.

propositions.text: Witness XXXX said minorities in Somalia try to ally with major tribes for protection.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX XXXX another witness for the Appellant at her hearing, indicated that people in the minority in Somalia try to ally themselves with major tribes who can protect them.

propositions.text: Appellant and husband owned a home in Mogadishu, sold before leaving; she attended Koranic school intermittently.
propositions.quote: Even though the Appellant alleges she was poor in Somalia, she and her husband owned a home in Mogadishu which they sold prior to leaving. She attended Koranic school, although intermittently.

propositions.text: Witness XXXX said she went to school in Somalia because her father had money.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX XXXX indicated at the hearing that she went to school in Somalia because her father had money.

propositions.text: The XXXX, though few and scattered, have allied with majority clans including Hawiye through lineage.
propositions.quote: The evidence suggests that the XXXX, although they are few in numbers and are scattered throughout Somalia, have allied themselves with one of the majority clans, including the Hawiye which they are affiliated through lineage.

propositions.text: The Appellant was not viewed as a member of a weak minority clan as alleged.
propositions.quote: The evidence also suggests that the Appellant was not viewed as a member of a weak minority clan as alleged.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the XXXX are aligned with a majority clan, supported by documentary and witness evidence, and the Appellant is not part of a weak minority clan as alleged.

propositions.text: Board members should avoid overzealous findings of inconsistencies in testimony of applicants using interpreters.
propositions.quote: The Appellant points to jurisprudence indicating that it is important for Board members to avoid being overzealous in the finding of inconsistencies in the testimony of applicants who are speaking through interpreters.

propositions.text: Appellant relied on an interpreter for both written BoC and oral testimony.
propositions.quote: She points out that she relied on an interpreter in her dealings with the Board with respect to both her written BoC and her oral testimony.

propositions.text: RPD drew negative credibility inferences from discrepancies between BoC, counsel's statement, and oral testimony.
propositions.quote: She notes that the RPD drew a number of negative inferences about her credibility on the basis of the discrepancies between her BoC, the statement that was proffered by her former counsel prior to the hearing, and her oral testimony.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues the Board was overzealous in finding inconsistencies due to interpreter use and drew negative credibility inferences improperly.

propositions.text: Appellant needed interpreter despite signing Declaration A indicating English understanding.
propositions.quote: The Appellant points out that she needed to testify through an interpreter at her hearing, despite having signed Declaration A on her BoC indicating that she understood English.

propositions.text: RPD wrongly attributed inconsistencies to Appellant's credibility instead of interpreter's carelessness or incompetence.
propositions.quote: She argues that, instead of associating such an obvious mistake to a faulty interpreter's carelessness, an interpreter who was also interpreting at the hearing, the RPD instead associated the inconsistencies to her credibility.

propositions.text: Evidence suggests interpreter carelessness or incompetence caused discrepancies, not Appellant's lack of truthfulness.
propositions.quote: She submits that the evidence suggests, at the minimum, carelessness on the part of the interpreter, and at the worst, incompetence in the services of the interpreter.

propositions.text: Discrepancies likely due to bad support during documentation, not lack of cooperation or truthfulness.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that, given the situation with the inappropriate interpretation, the discrepancies in her evidence, on a balance of probabilities, were more likely to be a result of bad support during the documentation period rather than her lack of cooperation or truthfulness.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues interpreter errors caused discrepancies, not her credibility, and that RPD wrongly blamed her instead of interpreter carelessness or incompetence.

propositions.text: Appellant called the individual she criticized as a witness on clan structure and women's treatment, not to address evidence anomalies.
propositions.quote: While the Appellant is critical of the individual who assisted her in the preparation of her forms, she called the same individual as a witness in her hearing to provide testimony regarding clan structure and the treatment of women in Somalia.

propositions.text: It is illogical Appellant would call a witness she was dissatisfied with to address anomalies, but she did not do so here.
propositions.quote: It does not make sense that the Appellant would call a witness she was dissatisfied with unless she was calling him to address anomalies in her evidence that he was allegedly responsible for. This was not the case here.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Appellant called the criticized individual as a witness on clans and women's treatment, not to address evidence anomalies.

propositions.text: Faulty interpretation does not explain many anomalies like vague testimony about husband's contact at refugee camp.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the allegedly faulty interpretation of forms does not explain many of the anomalies in the Appellant's evidence such as her vague testimony regarding contact with her husband at a refugee camp.

propositions.text: Appellant's claim that interpreter who helped with forms also interpreted at hearing is baseless.
propositions.quote: The Appellant's allegation that the interpreter who assisted her in the preparation of her forms was also the interpreter at her hearing is without basis as discussed above.

propositions.text: Appellant points to no interpretation errors during forms or hearing, only that she signed declaration in wrong place.
propositions.quote: Moreover, the Appellant fails to point out any errors in interpretation while completing her forms or at her hearing, simply relying on the fact that she signed her declaration in the wrong place to justify her allegation that the interpretation was faulty.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds faulty interpretation does not explain anomalies; Appellant's claim about interpreter overlap is baseless and no errors were pointed out.

propositions.text: RPD's findings were thorough, addressed significant claim aspects, and based on evidence; not overzealous in identifying inconsistencies.
propositions.quote: Having reviewed the record, in the RAD's opinion, the RPD's findings were thorough, addressed significant aspects of the claim, and were based on the evidence. The RPD was not overzealous in identifying inconsistencies in the Appellant's evidence.

propositions.text: RPD's findings support the conclusion reached in the Appellant's refugee protection claim.
propositions.quote: The following findings support the conclusion reached in the Appellant's claim for refugee protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD's findings thorough, evidence-based, not overzealous, and supporting the refugee protection claim conclusion.

propositions.text: Appellant said she had a sister at hearing but omitted her in BoC; explained sister was deceased but included deceased parents.
propositions.quote: The Appellant indicated at her hearing that she had a sister, however, she had not indicated that she had a sister in her BoC. She explained that she did not include her sister in her BoC because her sister is deceased; however, the Appellant's parents, who are also deceased, were included in the BoC.

propositions.text: Appellant's witness testified she had brothers and sisters; Appellant then said she has a brother and another sister.
propositions.quote: The Appellant's witness testified that the Appellant had brothers and sisters. When confronted with the information from the witness, the Appellant indicated that she has a brother and another sister.

propositions.text: Appellant said she omitted siblings in BoC because she only thought about husband and children when filling form.
propositions.quote: When asked about the prior omission of this information, the Appellant indicated that she was only thinking about her husband and children when she filled in the form and did not think about mentioning the brother or sister who might have been living but are missing.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds inconsistencies in Appellant's evidence about siblings, with unexplained omissions undermining credibility.

propositions.text: Instructions for BoC section 5 require listing relatives in order and providing death dates if deceased.
propositions.quote: Instructions for completing section 5 of the BoC are clear in asking refugee claimants to list their relatives in the following order: spouse, children, parents, brothers and sister. If a person is dead, the refugee claimant is instructed to provide the date of death.

propositions.text: It is reasonable to expect accurate, consistent family information; inconsistencies without explanation undermine credibility.
propositions.quote: It would be reasonable to expect the Appellant to provide accurate and consistent information regarding her family members as instructed. The inconsistencies and omissions in the Appellant's evidence regarding her siblings, without reasonable explanations, undermine her credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The court states BoC instructions require accurate family info; unexplained inconsistencies undermine Appellant's credibility.

propositions.text: Appellant's residence evidence is inconsistent between Schedule A and BoC narrative and testimony.
propositions.quote: The Appellant indicated in her Schedule A - Background/Declaration that she had resided in XXXX District, XXXX, XXXX, Somalia from XXXX 2004 until XXXX 2014. However, according to her BoC narrative and testimony at her hearing, the Appellant resided in Mogadishu from birth until XXXX 2013, when she went to reside with her husband's grandmother in XXXX.

propositions.text: Appellant blamed individuals who filled form but said info was read back to her for accuracy at hearing start.
propositions.quote: The Appellant attributed the inconsistency to the individuals who filled in her form; however, at the outset of her hearing, the Appellant indicated that the information on the forms had been read back to her to ensure accuracy.

propositions.text: Residence location before departure is significant due to al-Shabaab threats and home sale location.
propositions.quote: The location of the Appellant's residence in the two-year period before her departure from Somalia is a significant element of her story, particularly because the allegations regarding threats from members of al-Shabaab are specific to the area she was residing and the area where her husband sold their home.

propositions.text: Residence info relevant to whereabouts during alleged threats, safety, and connection to XXXX.
propositions.quote: The Appellant's residence information is relevant to her whereabouts at the time of the alleged threats, to her ability to live safely in Mogadishu, and her connection to XXXX.

propositions.text: Reasonable to expect consistent residence evidence; failure damages credibility further.
propositions.quote: It is reasonable to expect the Appellant to give consistent evidence about her residence, and her failure to do so further damages her credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Appellant's residence evidence inconsistent and important to her story, with failure to be consistent damaging credibility.

propositions.text: Appellant gave inconsistent evidence about attending Koranic school with witness; witness denied attending that school.
propositions.quote: The Appellant indicated at her hearing that she and her witness (XXXX XXXX XXXX) had gone to the same Koranic school in XXXX, Mogadishu. She first indicated that they attended the school together and later said that her witness had attended the school before her. She indicated that she did not remember playing with her witness when they were young children. On the other hand, the Appellant's witness indicated that she had never attended the Koranic school in XXXX and that she and the Appellant played together when all the cousins got together at their grandmother's house.

propositions.text: While full recall of childhood interactions is unreasonable, consistent evidence about school attendance is expected.
propositions.quote: Although it would be unreasonable to expect the Appellant and her witness to recall all their interactions with each other as children, one would expect them to provide consistent evidence regarding their attendance at a school in XXXX where the Appellant had indicated she and her witness had known each other.

propositions.text: Inconsistency further undermines Appellant's credibility.
propositions.quote: The inconsistency further undermines the Appellant's credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds inconsistent evidence about school attendance between Appellant and witness, undermining Appellant's credibility.

propositions.text: Appellant's BoC said husband's and children's whereabouts unknown; later said husband found a way to get children to safety.
propositions.quote: The Appellant indicated in her BoC that the whereabouts of her husband and children was unknown. According to her BoC narrative prepared the day before her hearing, the Appellant indicated that her husband found a way to get their children and they were all in a safe environment.

propositions.text: At hearing, Appellant said husband and children were at XXXX refugee camp but gave vague info on how they were located or reunited.
propositions.quote: At her hearing, the Appellant indicated that her husband and children were at the XXXX refugee camp. However, the Appellant failed to provide information about how her husband and children had been located, or how her husband and children were reunited, or how her husband and children had made their way to the XXXX refugee camp, even though the Appellant alleges to have spoken to her husband a number of times in the months before the hearing.

propositions.text: Appellant was vague when questioned about finding husband and children, giving meaningless responses.
propositions.quote: The Appellant was vague in her responses to questions about the new information about her husband and children. For instance, when asked how she learned that her husband and children were in the XXXX refugee camp, the Appellant said that she kept asking about her family and she was asking anyone who knew someone who would be able to help her. When asked to be more specific with her answer, the Appellant said that she had asked the lady who was with her in the community to help her look and find her family. She went on to say that it wasn't one person specifically and that it was a long process.

propositions.text: Such vague, meaningless responses about family location further undermine Appellant's credibility.
propositions.quote: The Appellant's meaningless responses related to finding her husband and children, when one would expect her to have and provide fulsome and detailed responses, further undermines the Appellant's credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Appellant gave vague, inconsistent testimony about husband and children's whereabouts, undermining her credibility.

propositions.text: RPD was correct to find Appellant did not establish she is XXXX or that XXXX are a weak, small sub clan.
propositions.quote: The RPD was not wrong to find that the Appellant had not satisfactorily established that she is necessarily XXXX or that the XXXX are a weak and small sub clan.

propositions.text: Evidence suggests XXXX allied with majority clans including Hawiye through lineage.
propositions.quote: As noted above, the evidence suggests that the XXXX have allied themselves with one of the majority clans, including the Hawiye which they are affiliated through lineage.

propositions.text: Evidence suggests Appellant was not viewed as member of weak minority clan as alleged.
propositions.quote: The evidence also suggests that the Appellant was not viewed as a member of a weak minority clan as alleged.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD correctly concluded Appellant did not establish weak minority clan membership; evidence shows alliance with majority clans.

propositions.text: RPD found it unreasonable Appellant and husband left six young sons with neighbour in town where al-Shabaab sought reprisals.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that it did not make sense that the Appellant and her husband would leave their six young sons under the care of a neighbour in the very town where al-Shabaab is allegedly seeking reprisals against the Appellant and her husband.

propositions.text: RAD concurs considering al-Shabaab's ruthlessness and propensity to abduct children; leaving children in harm's way is unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The RAD concurs with the RPD. Considering the ruthlessness of al-Shabaab and their propensity to abduct and forcibly recruit children, and considering the Appellant's allegation that al-Shabaab had come for her in XXXX, it is unreasonable that the Appellant would leave her six young children in harm's way in XXXX.

propositions.text: If al-Shabaab sought retaliation, Appellant's children would be likely targets; leaving them behind while fleeing is not credible.
propositions.quote: If al-Shabaab sought retaliation as alleged, the Appellant's six young children would be likely targets. If the Appellant and her husband were at risk of harm at the hands of al-Shabaab in XXXX, one would not expect the Appellant and her husband to leave their six young children in harm's way in XXXX while they fled.

propositions.text: On balance of probabilities, Appellant's allegation about leaving children behind is not credible.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant's allegation in this regard is not credible.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds it unreasonable and not credible that Appellant left six young children in harm's way while fleeing al-Shabaab threats.

propositions.text: RPD found Appellant's testimony vague about fleeing Mogadishu and why she had to abandon home and children.
propositions.quote: The RPD noted that the Appellant provided vague testimony about why she would choose to flee from Mogadishu, or why the people she was staying with there would be so sure that she was in danger from al-Shabaab in Mogadishu, that she would have to abandon her home and her children to leave on an uncertain trip away from her country at huge cost to herself and her family.

propositions.text: Appellant had friends in Mogadishu, $14,000 from husband, and lived there all her life.
propositions.quote: It noted that the Appellant had friends to stay with in Mogadishu, she allegedly had $14,000 given to her by her husband, and she was in a city where she had grown up and lived her whole life.

propositions.text: RPD found it did not make sense Appellant was unsafe in Mogadishu far from al-Shabaab in XXXX.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that it did not make sense that the Appellant was supposedly unable to safely remain in Mogadishu, far away from the al-Shabaab members in XXXX who allegedly wanted to find her.

propositions.text: RAD concurs; Appellant failed to explain why she had to flee Mogadishu despite safety, support, and funds there.
propositions.quote: The RAD concurs with the RPD. The Appellant was unable to adequately explain why she had to flee Mogadishu, when her evidence suggests that she was safe in that city from those who wanted to harm her, and she had the support of friends in Mogadishu, and she had the funds to support herself in that city.

propositions.text: On balance of probabilities, Appellant's allegation about fleeing Mogadishu is not credible.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant's allegation with respect to having to leave Mogadishu is not credible.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Appellant's vague testimony about fleeing Mogadishu is not credible given her safety, support, and funds there.

propositions.text: Appellant presented photos of injury alleged to be from escape from home in XXXX.
propositions.quote: The Appellant alleges that she injured herself while escaping from her home in XXXX. She presented photographs of her injury.

propositions.text: RPD found injury presence insufficient to establish overall credibility of Appellant's allegations.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the presence of an injury is not sufficient to establish the credibility of the Appellant's overall allegations.

propositions.text: RAD concurs; corroboration of injury does not make an incredible story credible.
propositions.quote: The RAD concurs with the RPD. The Appellant's story has been found to lack credibility and photographs corroborating an injury does not make her story credible. Corroboration does not make an incredible story credible.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds injury photos insufficient to establish credibility; corroboration does not make an incredible story credible.

propositions.text: RPD considered residual evidence including Appellant's profile as a female from Somalia.
propositions.quote: The RPD considered whether there was any residual evidence to support a claim for refugee protection; namely the Appellant's profile as a female from Somalia.

propositions.text: Minister noted Appellant did not claim refugee status based on gender alone and lived comfortably in Mogadishu with family for years.
propositions.quote: It was pointed out by the Minister that the Appellant had not alleged that she was a refugee based on her gender alone, and noted that the Appellant had apparently lived comfortably in Mogadishu with her husband and six children for years.

propositions.text: RPD noted Appellant did not establish vulnerability of clan affiliation.
propositions.quote: The RPD noted in its conclusion that the Appellant had not satisfactorily established the vulnerability of her clan affiliation.

propositions.text: Country documents reveal serious concerns with women's rights to education and personal autonomy in Somalia.
propositions.quote: It also noted that country documents reveal serious concerns with women's rights to education and personal autonomy in Somalia.

propositions.text: Evidence about Mogadishu is mixed: attacks exist but city has recovered security and former residents return.
propositions.quote: The RPD noted that the evidence about the situation in Mogadishu is mixed; there is evidence of attacks in Mogadishu while there is evidence that the city has recovered its liveliness and overall security and former residents have chosen to return.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes RPD considered residual evidence including gender profile; Minister noted no gender-only claim; evidence on Mogadishu is mixed.

propositions.text: Appellant was not forthcoming about identity and whereabouts of immediate family members.
propositions.quote: The RAD notes, as did the RPD, that the Appellant was not forthcoming about the identity and whereabouts of her immediate family members.

propositions.text: Appellant and family originate from Mogadishu, suggesting family and friends reside there.
propositions.quote: The fact that the Appellant and her family, as well as her husband and his family, originate from Mogadishu suggests that the Appellant has family and friends who reside in Mogadishu.

propositions.text: Appellant stayed with friends in Mogadishu before leaving Somalia, indicating support available there.
propositions.quote: The Appellant even indicated that she stayed with friends in Mogadishu before she left Somalia. This is indicative of the support that would be available to her in that city.

propositions.text: Appellant spent most of life in Mogadishu, suggesting familiarity with city.
propositions.quote: The fact that the Appellant spent most of her life in Mogadishu suggests that she is familiar with the city.

propositions.text: Appellant and husband owned home in Mogadishu, suggesting they were doing well there.
propositions.quote: The fact that she and her husband owned a home in Mogadishu suggests that they were doing well in that city.

propositions.text: Lack of credible evidence on Appellant's circumstances and family whereabouts hinders fuller risk analysis.
propositions.quote: The lack of credible evidence regarding the Appellant's circumstances and the whereabouts of family members hinders a more fulsome analysis of the Appellant's risk profile;

propositions.text: Based on above analysis, RAD finds Appellant does not face serious persecution risk in Mogadishu based on gender.
propositions.quote: however based on the analysis above, the RAD finds that the Appellant does not face a serious possibility of persecution in Mogadishu based on her gender.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Appellant was not forthcoming about family; evidence suggests support in Mogadishu; no serious persecution risk based on gender.

propositions.text: Appellant alleges inadequate interpretation, former counsel negligence, RPD overzealousness, and misapprehension of clan evidence.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has alleged that she received inadequate interpretation services, her former counsel was negligent, the RPD was overzealous in scrutinizing her testimony, and the RPD misapprehended the evidence regarding her clan.

propositions.text: RAD finds Appellant's allegations about interpretation and counsel baseless; RPD did not err in scrutiny or evidence appraisal.
propositions.quote: Based on its own analysis of the record, the RAD has found that the Appellant's allegations regarding interpretation and former counsel are baseless and the RPD did not err by being overzealous in scrutinizing or misapprehending her evidence.

propositions.text: RPD's findings are thorough and evidence-based; RAD reaches same conclusion as RPD.
propositions.quote: The RPD's findings are thorough and based on the evidence. Upon a review of the record, the RAD has reached the same conclusion as the RPD.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Appellant's allegations about interpretation, counsel, and RPD errors baseless; RAD agrees with RPD's thorough findings.

propositions.text: Due to anomalies in evidence, RAD finds Appellant lacks credibility.
propositions.quote: As a cumulative result of the above-noted anomalies in the Appellant's evidence, the RAD finds that the Appellant lacks credibility.

propositions.text: RAD does not accept on balance of probabilities that material events occurred as described by Appellant.
propositions.quote: The RAD does not accept, on a balance of probabilities, that the material events, as described by the Appellant in her Basis of Claim Form and at her hearing with the RPD, occurred as described.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Appellant lacks credibility and does not accept her material events on balance of probabilities.

propositions.text: Appellant has not established on balance of probabilities harm or threat by al-Shabaab members or sympathizers.
propositions.quote: On the basis of the findings noted above and after its own assessment of all the evidence in the record, including the recording of the hearing, the RAD finds that the Appellant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that she was harmed or threatened with harm by members or sympathizers of al-Shabaab.

propositions.text: Appellant has not established on balance of probabilities that she is part of a weak minority clan as alleged.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has not established on a balance of probabilities that she is part of a weak minority clan as alleged.

propositions.text: Residual evidence does not support a claim for refugee protection.
propositions.quote: The residual evidence does not support a claim for refugee protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes Appellant has not established harm or weak minority clan membership; residual evidence does not support refugee claim.

propositions.text: There is not a serious possibility of persecution if the Appellant returns to Somalia
propositions.quote: Therefore, the RAD finds that there is not a serious possibility of persecution should the Appellant return to Somalia.

propositions.text: The Appellant has failed to establish a well-founded fear of persecution under section 96 of the IRPA
propositions.quote: The RAD therefore concludes that the Appellant has failed to establish a well-founded fear of persecution under section 96 of the IRPA

propositions.text: The Appellant is not a person in need of protection or at risk of life, cruel treatment, or torture under section 97 of the IRPA
propositions.quote: the RAD finds that the Appellant is not a person in need of protection or at a risk to life, or at risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or in danger of torture as set out in section 97 of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds no serious possibility of persecution if the Appellant returns to Somalia and concludes she failed to establish a well-founded fear or need for protection under IRPA sections 96 and 97.

propositions.text: The Refugee Appeal Division confirms the Refugee Protection Division's decision and dismisses the appeal under section 111(1)(a) of the IRPA
propositions.quote: the Refugee Appeal Division confirms the decision of the Refugee Protection Division and dismisses the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD confirms the RPD decision and dismisses the appeal under section 111(1)(a) of the IRPA.
